claim: Il-1β was upregulated in the hypothalamus during PDAC at 10 days post-inoculation.
source: In agreement with our previous studies we observed that Il-1β was upregulated in the hypothalamus (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Il-1β was upregulated in the area postrema during PDAC at 10 days post-inoculation.
source: It was also upregulated in the area postrema, and showed a trend toward significance in the hippocampus (p=0.08).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Il-1β showed a trend toward significance in the hippocampus during PDAC at 10 days post-inoculation (p=0.08).
source: It was also upregulated in the area postrema, and showed a trend toward significance in the hippocampus (p=0.08).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Ptgs2 was upregulated in the hypothalamus and area postrema, but not the hippocampus during PDAC.
source: However, of the other cytokine transcripts analyzed, only those coding for prostaglandin synthase D2 (Ptgs2 – in the hypothalamus and area postrema, but not the hippocampus) and IL-1R (Il1r - again in the hypothalamus and area postrema, but not the hippocampus) were upregulated.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Il1r was upregulated in the hypothalamus and area postrema, but not the hippocampus during PDAC.
source: However, of the other cytokine transcripts analyzed, only those coding for prostaglandin synthase D2 (Ptgs2 – in the hypothalamus and area postrema, but not the hippocampus) and IL-1R (Il1r - again in the hypothalamus and area postrema, but not the hippocampus) were upregulated.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Il10 was upregulated in the area postrema only during PDAC.
source: The anti-inflammatory transcript Il10 was upregulated in the area postrema only.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Nos2 was downregulated in all three brain regions (hypothalamus, hippocampus, area postrema) during PDAC.
source: Interestingly, the transcript coding for nitric oxide synthase 2 (Nos2 – induced during inflammation and mainly expressed by endothelial cells) was downregulated in all three brain regions.

claim: Cxcl1 and Cxcl2 were highly upregulated in all three brain regions (hypothalamus, hippocampus, area postrema) during PDAC.
source: Two of the three IL-8 orthologues, Cxcl1 and Cxcl2, were highly upregulated in all three regions investigated.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Ccl2 was highly upregulated in the hippocampus during PDAC.
source: Ccl2 was highly upregulated in the hippocampus, and nearly significantly upregulated in the hypothalamus (p=0.06).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Ccl2 was nearly significantly upregulated in the hypothalamus during PDAC (p=0.06).
source: Ccl2 was highly upregulated in the hippocampus, and nearly significantly upregulated in the hypothalamus (p=0.06).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Cxcl9 was downregulated in both the area postrema and hypothalamus during PDAC.
source: Alternatively, Cxcl9 was downregulated in both the area postrema and hypothalamus, whereas Cxcl10 was downregulated in the area postrema, yet upregulated in the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Cxcl10 was downregulated in the area postrema during PDAC.
source: Alternatively, Cxcl9 was downregulated in both the area postrema and hypothalamus, whereas Cxcl10 was downregulated in the area postrema, yet upregulated in the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Cxcl10 was upregulated in the hippocampus during PDAC.
source: Alternatively, Cxcl9 was downregulated in both the area postrema and hypothalamus, whereas Cxcl10 was downregulated in the area postrema, yet upregulated in the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Cxcl5 was downregulated in the hippocampus during PDAC.
source: Lastly, the third IL-8 orthologue, Cxcl5, was downregulated in the hippocampus.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a significant increase in CD45highCD11b+ myeloid cells in the brains of animals with PDAC compared to sham-injected animals.
source: Compared to sham-injected animals, we observed a significant increase in CD45highCD11b+ myeloid cells in the brains of animals with PDAC (Figure 2B), with an increase as a percentage of total CD45+ (all immune cells) and CD45high (non-microglia leukocytes) cells occurring at 5 d.p.i. (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B, 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The increase in CD45highCD11b+ myeloid cells as a percentage of total CD45+ cells occurred at 5 days post-inoculation.
source: Compared to sham-injected animals, we observed a significant increase in CD45highCD11b+ myeloid cells in the brains of animals with PDAC (Figure 2B), with an increase as a percentage of total CD45+ (all immune cells) and CD45high (non-microglia leukocytes) cells occurring at 5 d.p.i. (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Both absolute and relative number of lymphocytes (CD45highCD11b-) were decreased in the brains of tumor animals compared to sham animals starting at 5 d.p.i.
source: Both absolute and relative number of lymphocytes (CD45highCD11b-) were decreased in the brains of tumor animals compared to sham animals starting at 5 d.p.i., which was driven by a decrease in B-cells and CD4+ T-cells (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The decrease in lymphocytes in the brains of tumor animals was driven by a decrease in B-cells and CD4+ T-cells.
source: Both absolute and relative number of lymphocytes (CD45highCD11b-) were decreased in the brains of tumor animals compared to sham animals starting at 5 d.p.i., which was driven by a decrease in B-cells and CD4+ T-cells (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was no change in number of microglia (defined as CD45midCD11b+) throughout the disease course.
source: There was no change in number of microglia (defined as CD45midCD11b+) throughout the disease course (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: By 7 d.p.i., there was an increase in relative number (as a percentage of total CD45+ and CD45high) of Ly6CmidLy6Ghigh neutrophils, Ly6Clow myeloid cells, and Ly6Chigh monocytes.
source: Further phenotypic analysis of infiltrating myeloid cells revealed that by 7 d.p.i., there was an increase in relative number (as a percentage of total CD45+ and CD45high) of Ly6CmidLy6Ghigh neutrophils, Ly6Clow myeloid cells, and Ly6Chigh monocytes (Figure 1D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D, 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was an increase in absolute number of neutrophils, Ly6Chigh monocytes, and Ly6Clow myeloid cells starting at 7 d.p.i., which became significant at either 7 (Ly6Chigh monocytes) or 10 d.p.i. (neutrophils and Ly6Clow myeloid cells).
source: We observed an increase in absolute number of neutrophils, Ly6Chigh monocytes, and Ly6Clow myeloid cells starting at 7 d.p.i., which became significant at either 7 (Ly6Chigh monocytes) or 10 d.p.i. (neutrophils and Ly6Clow myeloid cells) (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D and 2E, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Neutrophils were the most numerous invading myeloid cell type, constituting 34% of CD45highCD11b+ cells in sham animals, and increasing to nearly 54% by 10 d.p.i. in tumor animals.
source: Neutrophils were by far the most numerous invading myeloid cell type, constituting 34% percent of CD45highCD11b+ cells in sham animals, and increasing to nearly 54% by 10.d.p.i. in tumor animals (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: 95% of the population defined as 'microglia' expressed CX3CR1.
source: We observed that 95% of the population we defined as 'microglia' expressed CX3CR1, while only 6% of the population we defined as 'neutrophils' expressed this protein, confirming the identity of these cells as microglia and neutrophils, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Only 6% of the population defined as 'neutrophils' expressed CX3CR1.
source: We observed that 95% of the population we defined as 'microglia' expressed CX3CR1, while only 6% of the population we defined as 'neutrophils' expressed this protein, confirming the identity of these cells as microglia and neutrophils, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: GFP BMT mice exhibited 75% chimerism on average.
source: On average, mice that underwent bone marrow transplant (GFP BMT mice) exhibited 75% chimerism (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: At 10 d.p.i., thousands of GFP+ myeloid cells infiltrated the brain in tumor animals.
source: In agreement with results from WT marrow animals, we observed that at 10 d.p.i., thousands of GFP+ myeloid cells infiltrated the brain in tumor animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and D, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The majority of GFP+ infiltrating cells in the brain were neutrophils, with a concurrent increase in Ly6Chigh monocytes.
source: The majority of these cells were neutrophils, with a concurrent increase in Ly6Chigh monocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C-F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C-F and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a decrease in brain lymphocytes (CD45+GFP+CD11b-) in tumor animals at 10 d.p.i.
source: As we observed previously, this coincided with a decrease in brain lymphocytes (CD45+GFP+CD11b-) in tumor animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was no increase in GFP+ Ly6Clow myeloid cells in GFP BMT tumor animals.
source: We did not observe an increase in GFP+ Ly6Clow myeloid cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3F), suggesting that the increase in CD45highCD11b+Ly6Clow cells in our WT marrow PDAC mice was a result of microglia activation, rather than infiltrating monocytes.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3F and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The increase in CD45highCD11b+Ly6Clow cells in WT marrow PDAC mice was a result of microglia activation, rather than infiltrating monocytes.
source: We did not observe an increase in GFP+ Ly6Clow myeloid cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3F), suggesting that the increase in CD45highCD11b+Ly6Clow cells in our WT marrow PDAC mice was a result of microglia activation, rather than infiltrating monocytes.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of increase in GFP+ Ly6Clow myeloid cells in bone marrow chimera experiments, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3F.

claim: Myeloid cells infiltrate the brain during PDAC, temporally correlating with symptom onset.
source: Taken together, these data show that myeloid cells infiltrate the brain during PDAC, temporally correlating with symptom onset.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a conclusion from the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: The majority of infiltrating immune cells were neutrophils.
source: The majority of infiltrating immune cells were neutrophils.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a conclusion from the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2.

claim: There was a robust increase in leukocytes in the meninges adjacent to the hippocampus and median eminence in tumor mice at 10 d.p.i.
source: Although we observed scattered CD45+ globoid cells within the parenchyma in the cortex and thalamus in tumor mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we observed a robust increase in leukocytes in the meninges adjacent to the hippocampus and median eminence (ME) (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and C, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was an increase in overall CD45 immunoreactivity in the area postrema in tumor animals, but these cells appeared ramified rather than globoid.
source: While there was an increase in overall CD45 immunoreactivity in the area postrema, these cells appeared ramified rather than globoid (Figure 3D), suggesting microglia activation rather than immune cell infiltration.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The ramified appearance of CD45+ cells in the area postrema suggests microglia activation rather than immune cell infiltration.
source: While there was an increase in overall CD45 immunoreactivity in the area postrema, these cells appeared ramified rather than globoid (Figure 3D), suggesting microglia activation rather than immune cell infiltration.
evidence: Inferred from the morphological appearance of CD45+ cells in the area postrema as shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was an increase in neutrophils (defined as myeloperoxidase [MPO] positive, CD45+ globoid cells) only in the meninges surrounding the hippocampus (velum interpositum).
source: Interestingly, we observed an increase in neutrophils (defined as myeloperoxidase [MPO] positive, CD45+ globoid cells) only in the meninges surrounding the hippocampus (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The velum interpositum is a double-layered invagination of the pia matter.
source: This layer of meninges, known as the velum interpositum (VI), is a double-layered invagination of the pia matter.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a description of the anatomical structure.

claim: The velum interpositum is closed rostrally and communicates caudally with the quadrigeminal cistern.
source: This potential space is closed rostrally, communicates caudally with the quadrigeminal cistern, and is highly vascularized via a number of internal cerebral arterioles and veins.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a description of the anatomical structure.

claim: The velum interpositum is highly vascularized via a number of internal cerebral arterioles and veins.
source: This potential space is closed rostrally, communicates caudally with the quadrigeminal cistern, and is highly vascularized via a number of internal cerebral arterioles and veins.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a description of the anatomical structure.

claim: Recent studies demonstrate robust immune cell recruitment into the brain via the velum interpositum after mild trauma, during CNS infection, and during CNS autoimmune disease.
source: Recent studies demonstrate robust immune cell recruitment into the brain via this anatomical route after mild trauma, during CNS infection, and during CNS autoimmune disease (Alvarez and Teale, 2006; Schmitt et al., 2012; Szmydynger-Chodobska et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Alvarez and Teale, 2006; Schmitt et al., 2012; Szmydynger-Chodobska et al., 2016).

claim: Infiltrating neutrophils were present in the VI meninges in tumor mice.
source: We verified the presence of meninges in the VI with ER-TR7 labeling, which showed infiltrating neutrophils in the VI meninges in tumor mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Neutrophils in the VI were degranulating, with MPO 'blebs' present at the edge of many cells, along with extracellular MPO.
source: Neutrophils in the VI were degranulating, with MPO 'blebs' present at the edge of many cells, along with extracellular MPO (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Neutrophil degranulation was only present in brains of tumor animals and not in brains of sham animals.
source: This phenomenon was only present in brains of tumor animals and not in brains of sham animals.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) were present in the VI.
source: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) were also present in the VI, as identified by citrillunated histone H3 and MPO co-labeling (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: In the CNS parenchyma, especially in the thalamus and cortex, neutrophils were frequently observed undergoing phagocytosis by microglia.
source: In the CNS parenchyma, especially in the thalamus and cortex, we frequently observed neutrophils undergoing phagocytosis by microglia, with Iba-1+ cells extending processes around MPO+ neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Microglia protect the CNS parenchyma from neutrophil invasion during various states of inflammation.
source: This supports previous studies showing that microglia protect the CNS parenchyma from neutrophil invasion during various states of inflammation (Neumann et al., 2018; Neumann et al., 2008; Otxoa-de-Amezaga et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Neumann et al., 2018; Neumann et al., 2008; Otxoa-de-Amezaga et al., 2019).

claim: There was a large increase in GFP+ cells in the brains of KPC mice at 10 d.p.i. in GFP BMT mice.
source: In contrast, there was a large increase in GFP+ cells in the brains of KPC mice at 10 d.p.i.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The pattern of infiltrating GFP+ cells in GFP BMT mice was identical to CD45+ globoid cells in WT mice.
source: We observed a pattern of infiltrating GFP+ cells that was identical to CD45+ globoid cells in our previous experiments, with scattered GFP+ cells in the cortex and thalamus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), and accumulations of GFP+ cells in the VI (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: GFP+ cells were MPO+ in the VI in GFP BMT tumor mice.
source: In agreement with our previous data, GFP+ cells were MPO+ in the VI (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was complete abrogation of the population defined as neutrophils (CD45+CD11b+Ly6Cmid/highLy6Ghigh) in the circulation of 1A8-treated animals at 10 d.p.i.
source: At 10 d.p.i., there was complete abrogation of the population we defined as neutrophils (CD45+CD11b+Ly6Cmid/highLy6Ghigh) in the circulation of 1A8-treated animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and E, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was no decrease in CD45+CD11b+Dec205+CD115- neutrophils at 10 d.p.i. after daily treatment with 500 μg anti-Ly6G antibody.
source: Using this new definition for neutrophils, we observed that there was no decrease in this population at 10 d.p.i. after daily treatment with 500 μg anti-Ly6G antibody (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: During PDAC, chronic neutrophil depletion with anti-Ly6G antibody is not possible.
source: These results suggest that during PDAC, chronic neutrophil depletion with anti-Ly6G antibody is not possible.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a conclusion from the neutrophil depletion experiments.

claim: There was a decrease in CD45+ globoid cells in the VI in RS504393-treated tumor-bearing animals compared to vehicle-treated tumor-bearing animals.
source: We observed a decrease in CD45+ globoid cells in the VI in RS504393-treated tumor-bearing animals compared to vehicle-treated tumor-bearing animals (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B and C, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a slight decrease in CD45+ cells in the VI in SB225002-treated tumor-bearing animals compared to vehicle-treated tumor-bearing animals, but this difference was not significant.
source: Alternatively, while there was a slight decrease in CD45+ cells in the VI in SB225002-treated tumor-bearing animals compared to vehicle-treated tumor-bearing animals, this difference was not significant (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a moderate decrease in MPO+ cells in the VI in both SB225002- and RS504393-treated tumor-bearing animals compared to vehicle-treated tumor-bearing animals, but this difference was not significant.
source: Compared with vehicle-treated tumor-bearing animals, there was a moderate decrease in MPO+ cells in the VI in both SB225002- and RS504393-treated tumor-bearing animals, but this difference was also not significant.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the text.

claim: RS504393-treated animals experienced decreased anorexia, as evidenced by increased food intake, compared to vehicle-treated tumor-bearing animals.
source: While all groups consumed similar amounts of food over the first 7 days of the study (pre-cachexia) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), RS504393-treated animals experienced decreased anorexia, as evidenced by increased food intake, compared to vehicle-treated tumor-bearing animals (Figure 4E)
evidence: Supported by food intake data shown in Figure 4E and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: SB225002-treated tumor-bearing animals had similar food intake compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: Alternatively, SB225002-treated tumor-bearing had similar food intake compared to vehicle-treated animals.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the text.

claim: RS504393-treated animals had a nonsignificant increase in gastrocnemius mass compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: RS504393-treated animals had a nonsignificant increase in gastrocnemius mass compared to vehicle-treated animals, but did have an increase in heart mass compared to vehicle-treated animals, indicating decreased muscle catabolism (Figure 4F and G).

claim: RS504393-treated animals had an increase in heart mass compared to vehicle-treated animals, indicating decreased muscle catabolism.
source: RS504393-treated animals had a nonsignificant increase in gastrocnemius mass compared to vehicle-treated animals, but did have an increase in heart mass compared to vehicle-treated animals, indicating decreased muscle catabolism (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Supported by tissue mass data shown in Figure 4F and G, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was no difference in heart or gastrocnemius mass in SB225002-treated animals compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: There was no difference in heart or gastrocnemius mass in SB225002-treated animals compared to vehicle-treated animals.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was no difference in tumor mass in SB225002- or RS504393-treated animals compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: There was also no difference in tumor mass, or circulating immune cells in SB225002- or RS504393-treated animals compared to vehicle-treated animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by tumor mass data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was no difference in circulating immune cells in SB225002- or RS504393-treated animals compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: There was also no difference in tumor mass, or circulating immune cells in SB225002- or RS504393-treated animals compared to vehicle-treated animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by hematology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Pharmacologic inhibition of CCR2 is important for cachexia and immune cell recruitment to the brain during PDAC.
source: These data demonstrate that pharmacologic inhibition of CCR2 is important for cachexia and immune cell recruitment to the brain during PDAC.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a conclusion from the CCR2 inhibitor experiments.

claim: There was robust CCL2 mRNA expression exclusively within the VI during PDAC.
source: Using in situ hybridization we localized robust CCL2 mRNA expression exclusively within the VI during PDAC.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was no observable Ccl2 mRNA in the brains of sham animals.
source: There was no observable Ccl2 mRNA in the brains of sham animals (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: CCL2 protein was abundantly expressed in the VI in tumor animals at 10 d.p.i., exclusively expressed in Iba1+CD206+ meningeal macrophages.
source: We verified these results at the protein level using Ccl2mCherry mice, which showed abundant CCL2 protein expression in the VI in tumor animals at 10 d.p.i., exclusively expressed in Iba1+CD206+ meningeal macrophages.

claim: CCL2 protein was not expressed in VI meningeal macrophages in sham mice.
source: CCL2 protein was not expressed in VI meningeal macrophages in sham mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: At 10 d.p.i., CCR2+ immune cells infiltrated the brains of tumor mice and accumulated in the VI.
source: Ccr2RFP/WT reporter mice were used to localize CCR2+ cells in the CNS. We observed that, at 10 d.p.i., CCR2+ immune cells infiltrated the brains of tumor mice and accumulated in the VI (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: A large percentage of neutrophils in the VI were CCR2+.
source: Interestingly, a large percentage of neutrophils in the VI were CCR2+ (Figure 5D), which infiltrated throughout the VI and often formed large aggregates consisting of 20 cells or more (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: CCR2+ neutrophils infiltrated throughout the VI and often formed large aggregates consisting of 20 cells or more.
source: Interestingly, a large percentage of neutrophils in the VI were CCR2+ (Figure 5D), which infiltrated throughout the VI and often formed large aggregates consisting of 20 cells or more (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was minimal CCR2 expression on circulating neutrophils in sham animals.
source: As expected, we observed minimal CCR2 expression on circulating neutrophils in sham animals.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a slight increase in circulating CCR2+ neutrophils in tumor-bearing animals.
source: While there was a slight increase in circulating CCR2+ neutrophils in tumor-bearing animals, there was no increase in CCR2+ neutrophils in the liver.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was no increase in CCR2+ neutrophils in the liver in tumor-bearing animals.
source: While there was a slight increase in circulating CCR2+ neutrophils in tumor-bearing animals, there was no increase in CCR2+ neutrophils in the liver.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a large increase in CCR2+ neutrophils in the brains of tumor-bearing animals.
source: Alternatively, there was a large increase in CCR2+ neutrophils in the brains of tumor-bearing animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Ccl2 was by far the most robustly upregulated chemokine transcript (approximately 135-fold) in microglia treated with PDAC conditioned media.
source: We observed that, of the chemokine transcripts queried, Ccl2 was by far the most robustly upregulated (approximately 135-fold).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Cxcl1 and Cxcl2 were upregulated in microglia treated with PDAC conditioned media, but not as robustly as Ccl2 (15 and approximately 35-fold, respectively).
source: Cxcl1 and Cxcl2 were upregulated, but not nearly as robustly (15 and approximately 35-fold, respectively) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 were not induced in microglia treated with PDAC conditioned media.
source: Alternatively, Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 were not induced.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: LPS induced robust upregulation of all five chemokine transcripts (Ccl2, Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Cxcl9, Cxcl10) in microglia.

evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: PDAC-derived factors induce chemokine expression in brain macrophages.
source: These results demonstrate that PDAC-derived factors induce chemokine expression in brain macrophages, and, unlike LPS, there is preferential upregulation of certain chemokines, especially CCL2.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a conclusion from the in vitro microglia culture experiments.

claim: Unlike LPS, PDAC-derived factors cause preferential upregulation of certain chemokines, especially CCL2, in brain macrophages.
source: These results demonstrate that PDAC-derived factors induce chemokine expression in brain macrophages, and, unlike LPS, there is preferential upregulation of certain chemokines, especially CCL2.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a conclusion from the in vitro microglia culture experiments.

claim: At 11 d.p.i., there was a 37% decrease in total CD45high myeloid cells in the brains of CCR2KO tumor mice compared to WT tumor mice.
source: Using flow cytometry, we observed that at 11 d.p.i. after IP inoculation, there was a 37% decrease in total CD45high myeloid cells in the brains of CCR2KO tumor mice compared to WT tumor mice (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A and B, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The decrease in CD45high myeloid cells in CCR2KO tumor mice was driven by a large decrease in brain-infiltrating neutrophils and Ly6Chigh monocytes.
source: This difference was driven by a large decrease in brain-infiltrating neutrophils and Ly6Chigh monocytes.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a decrease in neutrophils and Ly6Chigh monocytes as a percentage of CD45high cells in the brains of CCR2KO tumor mice.
source: There was also decrease in neutrophils and Ly6Chigh monocytes as a percentage of CD45high cells in the brains of CCR2KO tumor mice, indicating that differences were not due to a global decrease in infiltrating immune cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There were no differences in microglia, Ly6Clow monocytes, or T-cells in the brains of CCR2KO tumor mice compared to WT tumor mice.
source: This was also supported by the fact that there were no differences in microglia (data not shown), Ly6Clow monocytes, or T-cells in the brains of CCR2KO tumor mice compared to WT tumor mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a dramatic decrease in both total CD45+ globoid and MPO+ immune cells in the VI in CCR2KO tumor mice compared to WT tumor mice.
source: Indeed, we observed a dramatic decrease in both total CD45+ globoid and MPO+ immune cells in the VI in CCR2KO tumor mice compared to WT tumor mice (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7D and E, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: CCR2KO mice had decreased anorexia during PDAC compared to WT tumor mice.
source: In agreement with our findings from pharmacologic inhibition of CCR2, we observed that CCR2KO mice had decreased anorexia during PDAC compared to WT tumor mice (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by food intake data shown in Figure 7F and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: CCR2KO tumor mice had attenuated muscle loss compared to WT tumor mice.
source: CCR2KO tumor mice also had attenuated muscle loss compared to WT tumor mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by gastrocnemius mass data shown in Figure 7G and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Compared to WT tumor animals, CCR2KO tumor animals had decreased induction of Murf1 and Foxo1.
source: We observed that, compared to WT tumor animals, CCR2KO tumor animals had decreased induction of Murf1 and Foxo1 (Figure 7H), confirming that there was decreased catabolic drive in CCR2KO tumor mice.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7H and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was decreased catabolic drive in CCR2KO tumor mice.
source: We observed that, compared to WT tumor animals, CCR2KO tumor animals had decreased induction of Murf1 and Foxo1 (Figure 7H), confirming that there was decreased catabolic drive in CCR2KO tumor mice.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7H and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a decrease in circulating Ly6Chigh monocytes in CCR2KO tumor mice.
source: We only observed a decrease in circulating Ly6Chigh monocytes in CCR2KO tumor mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The largest decrease in neutrophils in CCR2KO tumor mice was in the brain.
source: When we assessed neutrophils in CCR2KO tumor mice in different organs as a percentage of those in WT tumor mice, we found the largest decrease to be in the brain and observed a slight increase in circulating neutrophils in CCR2KO tumor mice compared to WT tumor mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and H), suggesting that the decrease in brain-infiltrating neutrophils was due to a homing defect rather than inability to mobilize from the bone marrow.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and H, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a slight increase in circulating neutrophils in CCR2KO tumor mice compared to WT tumor mice.
source: When we assessed neutrophils in CCR2KO tumor mice in different organs as a percentage of those in WT tumor mice, we found the largest decrease to be in the brain and observed a slight increase in circulating neutrophils in CCR2KO tumor mice compared to WT tumor mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and H), suggesting that the decrease in brain-infiltrating neutrophils was due to a homing defect rather than inability to mobilize from the bone marrow.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and H, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The decrease in brain-infiltrating neutrophils in CCR2KO tumor mice was due to a homing defect rather than inability to mobilize from the bone marrow.
source: When we assessed neutrophils in CCR2KO tumor mice in different organs as a percentage of those in WT tumor mice, we found the largest decrease to be in the brain and observed a slight increase in circulating neutrophils in CCR2KO tumor mice compared to WT tumor mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F and H), suggesting that the decrease in brain-infiltrating neutrophils was due to a homing defect rather than inability to mobilize from the bone marrow.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that circulating neutrophils were increased in CCR2KO tumor mice while brain-infiltrating neutrophils were decreased.

claim: CCR2 is important for neutrophil recruitment specifically to the brain during PDAC.
source: Therefore, our data show that CCR2 is important for neutrophil recruitment specifically to the brain, and that the decrease in brain-infiltrating neutrophils was due to a homing defect, rather than inability to mobilize from the bone marrow.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a conclusion from the CCR2KO experiments.

claim: Brain-infiltrating neutrophils clustered tightly together but were distinct from those in the liver, tumor, and blood based on principal component analysis of the top 500 most varying transcripts.
source: Principal component analysis of individual samples based on the top 500 most varying transcripts revealed that brain-infiltrating neutrophils clustered tightly together, but were distinct from those in the liver, tumor, and blood (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Over 100 transcripts were differentially expressed in brain-infiltrating neutrophils compared to those in the liver, tumor, and circulation.
source: Furthermore, we were able to identify over 100 transcripts that were differentially expressed in the brain-infiltrating neutrophils compared to those in the liver, tumor, and circulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C-E and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C-E and Figure 7—figure supplement 3, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: ICV oATP treatment completely prevented both neutrophils and total CD45high myeloid cells from infiltrating the brain.
source: oATP treatment completely prevented both neutrophils and total CD45high myeloid cells from infiltrating the brain (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a nonsignificant decrease in Ly6Chigh monocytes in oATP-treated tumor mice.
source: There was a nonsignificant decrease in Ly6Chigh monocytes in oATP-treated tumor mice (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Ly6Clow myeloid cells and T-cells were not affected by ICV oATP treatment.
source: Ly6Clow myeloid cells and T-cells were not affected (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: ICV oATP treatment did not affect any circulating immune cell population.
source: Furthermore, ICV oATP treatment did not affect any circulating immune cell population (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Both CD45+ globoid cells and CD45+MPO+ neutrophils in the VI were greatly decreased in oATP-treated tumor animals compared to aCSF-treated tumor animals.
source: When we investigated infiltrating immune cells in the VI, both CD45+ globoid cells and CD45+MPO+ neutrophils in the VI were greatly decreased in oATP-treated tumor animals compared to aCSF-treated tumor animals (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8C and D, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: oATP treatment attenuated anorexia in tumor mice.
source: We also observed that oATP treatment attenuated anorexia in tumor mice (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by food intake data shown in Figure 8E and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There was a trend toward increased gastrocnemius mass (p=0.09) in oATP-treated tumor mice compared to aCSF-treated tumor bearing mice.
source: There was trend toward increased gastrocnemius mass (p=0.09) in oATP-treated tumor mice compared to aCSF-treated tumor bearing mice (Figure 8F), which corresponded to a trend toward decreased induction of genes associated with proteolysis in gastrocnemius muscle (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating that muscle catabolism was moderately attenuated by oATP administration directly into the brain.
evidence: Supported by gastrocnemius mass data shown in Figure 8F and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Muscle catabolism was moderately attenuated by oATP administration directly into the brain.
source: There was trend toward increased gastrocnemius mass (p=0.09) in oATP-treated tumor mice compared to aCSF-treated tumor bearing mice (Figure 8F), which corresponded to a trend toward decreased induction of genes associated with proteolysis in gastrocnemius muscle (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating that muscle catabolism was moderately attenuated by oATP administration directly into the brain.
evidence: Supported by gastrocnemius mass data shown in Figure 8F and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Tumor size in oATP-treated tumor mice was identical to that of aCSF-treated tumor mice.
source: Tumor size in oATP-treated tumor mice was identical to that of aCSF-treated tumor mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by tumor mass data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There were no differences in microglia size, Iba-1 staining area, and Iba-1 intensity per cell when comparing aCSF- or oATP-treated tumor animals to oATP-treated sham animals or each other.
source: We did not observe any differences in microglia size, Iba-1 staining area, and Iba-1 intensity per cell when comparing aCSF- or oATP-treated tumor animals to oATP-treated sham animals or each other (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by microglia morphology data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B, and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: There were no differences in expression of Tnf, Cd68, Tmem119, P2y12, and P2x7r in oATP-treated tumor-bearing animals compared to aCSF-treated tumor-bearing animals.
source: We observed no differences in expression of Tnf, Cd68, Tmem119, P2y12, and P2x7r in oATP-treated tumor-bearing animals compared to aCSF-treated tumor-bearing animals (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C and explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Myeloid cells, consisting predominately of neutrophils, infiltrate the brain in a CCR2-dependent manner during PDAC, where they drive anorexia and muscle catabolism.
source: Our data show that in a mouse model of PDAC, myeloid cells, consisting predominately of neutrophils, infiltrate the brain, in a CCR2-dependent manner, where they drive anorexia and muscle catabolism.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a summary conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: Infiltrating immune cells accumulated specifically in the velum interpositum, which is adjacent to the hippocampus and the habenula.
source: We observed that infiltrating immune cells accumulated specifically in a unique layer of meninges called the velum interpositum (VI), which is adjacent to the hippocampus and the habenula, the latter of which is important for appetite regulation and is associating with cachexia in humans (Maldonado et al., 2018).
evidence: Explicitly stated in the Discussion section, with citation to Maldonado et al., 2018.

claim: The habenula is important for appetite regulation and is associated with cachexia in humans.
source: We observed that infiltrating immune cells accumulated specifically in a unique layer of meninges called the velum interpositum (VI), which is adjacent to the hippocampus and the habenula, the latter of which is important for appetite regulation and is associating with cachexia in humans (Maldonado et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maldonado et al., 2018.

claim: The VI is implicated as a key structure for initial immune infiltration during states of neuroinflammation such as EAE and traumatic brain injury.
source: The VI is implicated as a key structure for initial immune infiltration during states of neuroinflammation such as EAE (Schmitt et al., 2012) and traumatic brain injury (Szmydynger-Chodobska et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmitt et al., 2012 and Szmydynger-Chodobska et al., 2016.

claim: The VI contains the pial microvessels that are a key aspect of the 'gateway reflex', a neuro-immune pathway that involves interactions between leukocytes and neurons involved in stress response.
source: Indeed, the VI contains the pial microvessels that are a key aspect of the 'gateway reflex', a neuro-immune pathway that involves interactions between leukocytes and neurons involved in stress response (Tanaka et al., 2017) and is implicated in gastrointestinal dysfunction during EAE (Arima et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 2017 and Arima et al., 2017.

claim: The gateway reflex is implicated in gastrointestinal dysfunction during EAE.
source: Indeed, the VI contains the pial microvessels that are a key aspect of the 'gateway reflex', a neuro-immune pathway that involves interactions between leukocytes and neurons involved in stress response (Tanaka et al., 2017) and is implicated in gastrointestinal dysfunction during EAE (Arima et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arima et al., 2017.

claim: Neutrophils infiltrate the brain after septic doses of LPS or sepsis induced by cecal ligation.
source: While previous reports show that neutrophils infiltrate the brain after septic doses of LPS or sepsis induced by cecal ligation (He et al., 2016), it is still unknown if they contribute to neurologic sequelae (anorexia, fatigue, cognition and memory deficits, etc.) during and after sepsis.
evidence: Supported by citation to He et al., 2016.

claim: It is still unknown if neutrophils contribute to neurologic sequelae (anorexia, fatigue, cognition and memory deficits, etc.) during and after sepsis.
source: While previous reports show that neutrophils infiltrate the brain after septic doses of LPS or sepsis induced by cecal ligation (He et al., 2016), it is still unknown if they contribute to neurologic sequelae (anorexia, fatigue, cognition and memory deficits, etc.) during and after sepsis.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the Discussion section.

claim: 'Sickness behaviors' could be attenuated if myeloid cell recruitment to the brain was abrogated via administration of a P-selectin inhibitor in a mouse model of inflammatory liver disease.
source: A series of studies utilizing a mouse model of inflammatory liver disease showed that 'sickness behaviors' could be attenuated if myeloid cell recruitment to the brain was abrogated via any one of several different interventions, including: 1) administration of a P-selectin inhibitor (Kerfoot et al., 2006), 2) deleting Ccr2 (D'Mello et al., 2009), and 3) inhibiting microglia activation with minocycline (D'Mello et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kerfoot et al., 2006.

claim: 'Sickness behaviors' could be attenuated if myeloid cell recruitment to the brain was abrogated via deleting Ccr2 in a mouse model of inflammatory liver disease.
source: A series of studies utilizing a mouse model of inflammatory liver disease showed that 'sickness behaviors' could be attenuated if myeloid cell recruitment to the brain was abrogated via any one of several different interventions, including: 1) administration of a P-selectin inhibitor (Kerfoot et al., 2006), 2) deleting Ccr2 (D'Mello et al., 2009), and 3) inhibiting microglia activation with minocycline (D'Mello et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Mello et al., 2009.

claim: 'Sickness behaviors' could be attenuated if myeloid cell recruitment to the brain was abrogated via inhibiting microglia activation with minocycline in a mouse model of inflammatory liver disease.
source: A series of studies utilizing a mouse model of inflammatory liver disease showed that 'sickness behaviors' could be attenuated if myeloid cell recruitment to the brain was abrogated via any one of several different interventions, including: 1) administration of a P-selectin inhibitor (Kerfoot et al., 2006), 2) deleting Ccr2 (D'Mello et al., 2009), and 3) inhibiting microglia activation with minocycline (D'Mello et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Mello et al., 2013.

claim: Brain-infiltrating myeloid cells are key players in driving CNS-mediated signs and symptoms during inflammatory disease.
source: Therefore, our results, along with previous studies, implicate brain-infiltrating myeloid cells as key players in driving CNS-mediated signs and symptoms during inflammatory disease.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section, integrating current results with previous studies.

claim: PDAC reprograms macrophages, effectively impairing their phagocytic capabilities.
source: Moreover, previous studies demonstrated that PDAC reprograms macrophages, effectively impairing their phagocytic capabilities (Liu et al., 2019; Mantovani and Sica, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2019 and Mantovani and Sica, 2010.

claim: Macrophage phagocytosis is required for Ly6G antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion.
source: Since macrophage phagocytosis was shown to be required for Ly6G antibody-mediated neutrophil depletion (Bruhn et al., 2016), this may explain why the Ly6G antibody bound to neutrophils, but they were not depleted.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bruhn et al., 2016.

claim: Hypothalamic microglia were implicated in orchestrating a multicellular hypothalamic immune response, including infiltrating myeloid cells, during high fat diet-induced obesity.
source: Hypothalamic microglia were previously implicated in orchestrating a multicellular hypothalamic immune response, including infiltrating myeloid cells, during high fat diet-induced obesity (Valdearcos et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valdearcos et al., 2017.

claim: CCR2KO mice exhibited attenuated monocyte infiltration into the brain, along with decreased sickness behaviors during inflammatory liver disease.
source: Regardless, our results are in agreement with previous studies investigating sickness behaviors during inflammatory liver disease, which showed that CCR2KO mice exhibited attenuated monocyte infiltration into the brain, along with decreased sickness behaviors (D'Mello et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to D'Mello et al., 2009.

claim: Mice lacking Ccr2 had decreased myeloid cell infiltration into the brain and attenuated cognitive impairment during a model of sepsis induced by Streptococcus pneumoniae injection into the lungs.
source: Furthermore, it was recently reported that mice lacking Ccr2 had decreased myeloid cell infiltration into the brain and attenuated cognitive impairment during a model of sepsis induced by Streptococcus pneumoniae injection into the lungs (Andonegui et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Andonegui et al., 2018.

claim: CCL2 was identified as the only cytokine or chemokine (out of a panel of 25) that was increased in the serum of cachectic PDAC patients but not increased in the serum of non-cachectic patients.
source: In an attempt to identify inflammatory biomarkers for PDAC-associated cachexia, Talbert et al. identified CCL2 as the only cytokine or chemokine (out of a panel of 25) that was increased in the serum of cachectic PDAC patients but not increased in the serum of non-cachectic patients (Talbert et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Talbert et al., 2018.

claim: CCR2 is important for neutrophil chemotaxis during sepsis.
source: While CCR2 is usually not considered a key receptor for neutrophil recruitment, previous studies show it is important for neutrophil chemotaxis during sepsis (Souto et al., 2009; Souto et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Souto et al., 2009 and Souto et al., 2011.

claim: The CNS induces a more 'inflammatory' transcriptional profile in infiltrating myeloid cells compared to those that infiltrate other organs.
source: It was previously demonstrated that the CNS induces a more 'inflammatory' transcriptional profile in infiltrating myeloid cells compared to those that infiltrate other organs (Spath et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spath et al., 2017.

claim: Both the CCR2/CCL2 axis and neutrophils are reported to be 'pro-tumor'.
source: However, both the CCR2/CCL2 axis and neutrophils are reported to be 'pro-tumor' (Coffelt et al., 2016; Qian et al., 2011) and therefore systemic treatment targeting neutrophils or the CCR2/CCL2 axis in humans may be particularly beneficial in that they decrease tumor size and abrogate CNS dysfunction.
evidence: Supported by citations to Coffelt et al., 2016 and Qian et al., 2011.

claim: Chemotherapy and checkpoint inhibitors are both known to cause cachexia-like symptoms.
source: This would be advantageous to conventional anti-tumor therapies such as chemotherapy and checkpoint inhibitors, which are both known to cause cachexia-like symptoms (Braun et al., 2014; Michot et al., 2016) and not effective against PDAC.
evidence: Supported by citations to Braun et al., 2014 and Michot et al., 2016.

claim: Chemotherapy and checkpoint inhibitors are not effective against PDAC.
source: This would be advantageous to conventional anti-tumor therapies such as chemotherapy and checkpoint inhibitors, which are both known to cause cachexia-like symptoms (Braun et al., 2014; Michot et al., 2016) and not effective against PDAC.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Preventing myeloid cells from infiltrating the brain attenuates anorexia and muscle catabolism during PDAC.
source: In summary, we demonstrated that myeloid cells infiltrate the CNS throughout the course of PDAC and that preventing myeloid cells from infiltrating the brain attenuates anorexia and muscle catabolism.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a summary conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: There are distinct mechanisms for immune cell recruitment to the brain during systemic inflammation.
source: We showed there are distinct mechanisms for immune cell recruitment to the brain during systemic inflammation, and demonstrated a novel role for CCR2 in neutrophil recruitment to the brain, providing key insights into mechanisms of neuroinflammation and associated symptoms.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a summary conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: CCR2 has a novel role in neutrophil recruitment to the brain during PDAC.
source: We showed there are distinct mechanisms for immune cell recruitment to the brain during systemic inflammation, and demonstrated a novel role for CCR2 in neutrophil recruitment to the brain, providing key insights into mechanisms of neuroinflammation and associated symptoms.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a summary conclusion in the Discussion section.
